historical_timeline.summary: Born Gaius Julius Caesar in Rome.
His father dies suddenly in the morning, with no cause recorded.
In hiding from Sulla's agents while ill with a quartan fever.
His daughter Julia dies in childbirth.
Plutarch places his first epileptic fit at Corduba in Spain; Suetonius records fainting fits and nightmares towards the end of his life and two attacks of the falling sickness on campaign.

date.display: 6 April 46 BC in the old Roman calendar (about 7 February 46 BC, Julian)

historical_timeline.summary: Battle of Thapsus; by one account his usual sickness seized him and he was carried to a tower.

date.display: July to early November 46 BC (old Roman calendar)

historical_timeline.summary: In Rome: four triumphs within a month; the long year of 445 days that realigned the calendar.
Does not rise for the senators and blames his illness; Plutarch doubts the excuse.
Assassinated at a meeting of the Senate in Rome.

claims.statement: Gaius Julius Caesar was born on 12 or 13 July 100 BC in the Subura district of Rome, into the patrician family of the Julii.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The day and year rest on later ancient testimony; the date is in the pre-Julian Roman calendar.

claims.statement: Suetonius writes that he lost his father 'in the course of his sixteenth year'.
Pliny the Elder records that two men of the family, one of them his father, a former praetor, 'died without any apparent cause, in the morning, while putting on their shoes'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cause of death is not recorded. Modern writers have read these sudden deaths as cardiovascular deaths or as sudden death in epilepsy; both readings are retrospective.

claims.statement: As a young man, in hiding from Sulla's agents, he was 'suffering from a severe attack of quartan ague' and changed his hiding place almost every night.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A fever recurring every fourth day; modern readers usually take quartan fever to be malaria. Not used as a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: Plutarch describes him as 'of a spare habit', with 'a soft and white skin', and says he 'suffered from distemper in the head, and was subject to epileptic fits', the first of which attacked him at Corduba; he made 'his military service a cure for his feeble health'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Plutarch wrote about a century and a half later. The Corduba attack is not dated.

claims.statement: Suetonius says he was tall, of sound health, 'except that towards the end he was subject to sudden fainting fits and to nightmare as well', and that he was 'twice attacked by the falling sickness' (comitialis morbus) during his campaigns.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The ancient term comitialis morbus is usually translated as epilepsy, but it covered any falling attack; the description fits several modern diagnoses.

source_links.locator: Comitiali quoque morbo bis inter res agendas correptus est

claims.statement: Plutarch gives a second account of the battle of Thapsus in Africa in 46 BC, in which 'his usual sickness laid hold of him' as he was drawing up his army, and, sensing it coming, he was carried to a nearby tower and stayed there during the battle.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Plutarch reports this only as what others say; it may not have happened. The battle is dated 6 April 46 BC in the pre-Julian Roman calendar, about 7 February 46 BC in Julian terms.

claims.statement: When he did not rise to receive the senators, he afterwards 'made his disease an excuse', saying that the senses of those so afflicted do not stay steady when they address a standing crowd, with giddiness and insensibility; Plutarch says the excuse was not true.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An episode late in his life, after the period of the modern episode. Plutarch himself doubts the illness was the reason.

claims.statement: He drank very little wine: 'not even his enemies denied' it.
His only daughter, Julia, died in childbirth in 54 BC.
After the African campaign he returned to Rome in July 46 BC, celebrated four triumphs within a single month, and left Rome for Further Spain early in November 46 BC.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places him in Rome for the whole true frame of the modern episode.

claims.statement: He reformed the Roman calendar, which had drifted so far that the harvest festivals no longer came in summer, to a year of 365 days with a day added every fourth year; to realign it he lengthened 46 BC to 445 days, and the new calendar took effect on 1 January 45 BC.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Dates in 46 BC and earlier are in the old Roman calendar and cannot be converted exactly; early Julian dates before about 8 BC are also uncertain by a day or so because leap years were at first inserted every third year.

claims.statement: Retrospective readings take the attacks as epilepsy: one review counts four attacks that were probably complex partial (focal impaired-awareness) seizures and suggests an inherited cause; another treats them as late-onset epilepsy beginning at about 54 and proposes neurocysticercosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective diagnoses from ancient texts; neither can be tested.

claims.statement: Galassi and Ashrafian (2015) argued that his symptoms (headache, vertigo, falls, limb weakness, the collapse at Thapsus, and the giddiness at the Senate) fit cerebrovascular disease with transient ischemic attacks better than epilepsy, and that the sudden deaths in his family suggest cardiovascular disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective reading reported in a short article and in press coverage; it is one of several unresolved hypotheses.

claims.statement: Other proposed causes include a brain arteriovenous malformation, a brain tumor such as a meningioma, celiac disease, and malaria.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Each rests on the same few ancient passages.

claims.statement: He was assassinated on 15 March 44 BC, the Ides of March, at a meeting of the Senate in Rome, stabbed 23 times; the physician Antistius judged that only the second wound, in the breast, was mortal. Suetonius says he died 'in the fifty-sixth year of his age'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: He was 55. The date is in the new Julian calendar.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation of recurrent transient episodes of collapse in a 54-year-old man, separating seizure from convulsive syncope and transient ischemic attack (history from a witness, orthostatic vital signs, ECG and ambulatory cardiac monitoring under the ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 syncope guideline; EEG and MRI with diffusion-weighted and epilepsy-protocol sequences; CT angiography of the head and neck and echocardiography), and the diagnosis of late-onset focal epilepsy with a structural vascular cause from a clinically unrecognized cortical infarct, classified by the ILAE 2017 seizure and epilepsy classifications and the ILAE 2014 practical definition. Management follows the AAN/AES 2015 first-seizure guideline (recurrence risk and the case for treatment), the AAN/AES 2018 guideline on newer antiseizure medicines (levetiracetam, with mood monitoring), and the AHA/ASA 2021 secondary stroke prevention guideline with the CMID stroke, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia monographs (aspirin, high-intensity atorvastatin to an LDL below 70 mg/dL, blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg, 30-day rhythm monitoring, depression and cognitive screening), together with seizure safety and driving restrictions, an intercurrent respiratory infection, and an adult preventive visit. The historical dispute between epilepsy and cerebrovascular disease stays unresolved (R); the modern episode makes no claim about what he had.

hpi.narrative: Julius Caesar returns two weeks after his first visit. He saw Dr. Lindqvist-Adeyemi of neurology this morning. He has had no further spell, though he woke once from a vivid, frightening dream, confused for a minute or two, which happens every few weeks. The EEG showed intermittent left temporal sharp waves. The MRI showed no new stroke but an old small infarct in the left posterior temporal lobe and moderate small-vessel white matter changes, with no tumor, vascular malformation, or cyst. CT angiography showed a small calcified plaque at the left carotid bifurcation, under 30 percent. The echocardiogram showed mild left ventricular thickening, no clot, and no shunt. The 14-day monitor showed sinus rhythm throughout; the one event he marked, light-headedness on standing up quickly, was in sinus rhythm. He has taken lisinopril every morning without cough or dizziness but did not keep the home blood pressure log. He has not driven, has showered rather than bathed, and has not ridden. He wants to know what the spells are and when he can drive again.

referral.pertinent_history: Julius Caesar is a 54-year-old senior official and author. Six days ago, while standing for a long time at an outdoor ceremony on a hot day, he felt a strange rising feeling in the upper abdomen and dizziness, then collapsed; a member of his staff saw his eyes open and both arms stiffen and then jerk for about a minute. He bit the side of his tongue and was confused for about twenty minutes; paramedics took him to an emergency department, where a CT scan of the head, glucose, and sodium were normal, and he was sent home to arrange follow-up. About eighteen months ago, at a long dinner, he stared and smacked his lips for about a minute without responding, then was muddled; about six months ago, at an outdoor event abroad, he felt the same rising feeling and had to be helped into a nearby building, where he sat unaware of those around him for a minute or two. He has occasional mild headaches and vivid dreams that wake him. Hypertension told three years ago, never treated: 152/94 and 148/92 mmHg today, no orthostatic drop. Neurological examination normal. Today's tests: hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL; sodium 139 mmol/L; calcium 9.4 mg/dL; glucose 96 mg/dL; creatinine 0.98 mg/dL; HbA1c 5.6 percent; LDL 158 mg/dL; TSH 1.8. consultant_note.history: Julius Caesar is seen at the request of Dr. Fairbanks-Okonkwo, two weeks after a witnessed collapse. I took a fuller history from him and from the member of his staff who saw the latest spell. All three spells began with the same rising feeling in the upper abdomen, sometimes with a sense that things were strange or familiar; in two he stared and smacked his lips for a minute or so without responding; in the latest the arms then stiffened and jerked for about a minute. Each was followed by confusion of many minutes, and the latest by a bitten tongue and sore shoulders. None began with pallor, sweating, or greying vision, and none followed pain or a sudden change of posture; he had been standing for a long time in heat at the last. He has never had a sudden weakness, numbness, loss of speech, or loss of vision lasting minutes. He wakes every few weeks from vivid, frightening dreams, confused for a minute or two. He has occasional mild headaches. No head injury, meningitis, or febrile seizures in childhood that he knows of. He has had no spell since the first visit. He does not drive at present

assessment.display: Focal epilepsy with a structural vascular cause
assessment.assessment: These are seizures. The stereotyped rising epigastric aura, staring with oral automatisms, and prolonged confusion are typical of focal seizures from the temporal lobe, and the latest evolved to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Convulsive syncope is brief, follows a prodrome of pallor and greying vision, and recovers within a minute or two; his rhythm, echocardiogram, and orthostatic readings are normal. Transient ischemic attacks cause loss of function, not loss of awareness with automatisms. ILAE 2017: focal impaired-awareness seizures with automatisms and a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure; structural (vascular) cause. Three unprovoked seizures meet the ILAE definition of epilepsy; the brain lesion and the epileptiform EEG both raise the risk of recurrence. The vivid dreams with confused awakening may be nocturnal seizures and should go in the seizure diary

assessment.assessment: The left temporal infarct matches the EEG and is the likely seizure focus. It was never recognized as a stroke, but because it now causes epilepsy I would not treat it as a silent infarct; I advise secondary stroke prevention as after an ischemic stroke of undetermined cause. No source of embolism so far; prolonged monitoring is still needed for atrial fibrillation. Moderate white matter disease fits long-standing untreated hypertension
The main modifiable cause of his small-vessel disease; the target is below 130/80 mmHg

recommendations: Start levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily today: effective for focal seizures, no titration needed, and no interactions with his other medicines. Warn about irritability and low mood, check mood at four weeks, and keep a seizure diary. Lamotrigine is the alternative if mood side effects occur
Aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 80 mg at bedtime, with a lipid panel at 4 to 12 weeks and an LDL target below 70 mg/dL; dual antiplatelet therapy is not indicated for an old infarct
Blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg: continue lisinopril and add a second medicine, such as amlodipine, if he stays above target
A second ambulatory monitor for at least four more weeks, for more than 30 days in all, to exclude atrial fibrillation before settling on aspirin alone
Screen for sleep apnea (STOP-Bang, with a home sleep test if intermediate or high), check mood with the PHQ-9, and screen cognition with the MoCA in the first months

No driving until he has been seizure-free for the period state law requires (six months in this state) and I have cleared him; no swimming or riding alone, no climbing to heights, showers rather than baths, regular sleep, and a written seizure action plan for his staff, with emergency services called for a seizure lasting more than five minutes or a second seizure
Neurology review at six months, sooner for any seizure
